nameStory: The Red-gilled Nudibranch gets its name from the distinctive reddish projections called cerata that extend from its back, which function like external gills for breathing. The word 'nudibranch' literally means 'naked gills' in Latin, referring to these exposed breathing structures that make this group of sea slugs so distinctive.
description: The Red-gilled Nudibranch is a small, translucent sea slug that glides gracefully along the ocean floor and underwater surfaces. These delicate marine creatures have soft, jelly-like bodies that are typically whitish or clear, earning them the alternate name 'milky white sea slug.' They're quite small, usually less than an inch long, with finger-like projections extending from their backs. Like all nudibranchs, they're shell-less mollusks related to snails, but adapted for a completely aquatic lifestyle.

idTips.label: Red-tipped cerata
idTips.description: The most distinctive feature - numerous finger-like projections extending from the back that are clear to white at the base with bright reddish-orange tips, feeling soft and jelly-like if gently touched

idTips.label: Translucent body
idTips.description: Body appears milky white to completely transparent, allowing you to sometimes see internal structures through the skin like a living piece of sea glass

idTips.label: Smooth gliding movement
idTips.description: Moves with a characteristic smooth, flowing motion across surfaces using its muscular foot, leaving no visible slime trail unlike terrestrial slugs

idTips.label: Two tentacle-like rhinophores
idTips.description: Head features two sensory tentacles (rhinophores) that are often slightly clubbed at the tips and used for detecting chemicals in the water

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Typically less than an inch in total length, making them easy to overlook among seaweed and other marine growth

habitat: Red-gilled Nudibranchs inhabit shallow marine waters along New England's rocky coastline, typically found in tide pools and on underwater surfaces during low tide. They prefer areas with good water circulation and often crawl on seaweed, rocks, and dock pilings in harbors and protected bays. Look for them in depths from the low tide line down to about 30 feet, especially where there's plenty of marine growth to provide food and shelter.

seasonality.spring: More active as water temperatures begin to warm, often found in shallow tide pools during the lowest spring tides when they're easier to spot.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most likely to be observed feeding and moving about in warmer waters. Best viewing during calm days at low tide.
seasonality.fall: Still active in early fall but may move to slightly deeper water as temperatures drop. Continue checking tide pools during exceptionally low tides.
seasonality.winter: Much less active and rarely seen, likely moving to deeper waters or becoming dormant in protected crevices until spring returns.

funFact: Red-gilled Nudibranchs can steal the stinging cells from the hydroids they eat and incorporate them into their own cerata, essentially turning themselves into living weapons using their prey's own defenses - it's like eating spicy food and then breathing fire!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small, translucent nudibranchs in tide pools, but the bright red or orange tips on the cerata are usually diagnostic. Remember: 'Red tips on clear fingers' - if you see that combination, you've found your Red-gilled Nudibranch.
contextualKnowledge: This species goes by several common names including 'milky white sea slug' and 'pellucid aeolid,' but none are widely standardized, so you might see different names in various field guides. The scientific name 'pellucida' means transparent or translucent, referring to the see-through quality of the body.
compareHints: Since this is the only Carronella species recorded in New England waters, compare it with other aeolid nudibranchs in the family Flabellinidae by looking for the distinctive red-tipped cerata. Most other similar species either lack the bright red coloration on their projections or have different body colors and patterns.
